## Market Drone Strike Kills at Least 150 as Sudanese Fighters Hit Civilians

Struggling against each other on the battlefield, the sides in Sudan’s civil war are relying on drones to strike across vast distances, inflicting huge tolls on civilians in the process.

Listen

· 5:39 min

Video

More Than 150 Killed After Drone Strikes Disputed Sudanese Town

A drone strike on a market in Abyei, a disputed region between Sudan and South Sudan, killed at least 153 people on Monday, a local official said. Officials blamed Sudan’s military for the attack. Correction: An earlier version of this video appeared with an incorrect summary. Officials blamed Sudan’s military for the drone strikes, not the South Sudan government.Credit Credit...Aweil News Agency, via Associated Press

Oct. 21, 2026 Updated 12:51 p.m. ET

The drone attack struck a market without warning, sparking an inferno and sending oily smoke skyward. Those who could, scrambled to escape the heat. Many others stood no chance.

The attack on Monday on Amiet market in Abyei, a region disputed between Sudan and South Sudan and contested by the factions in Sudan’s civil war, caused particular shock because it hit a civilian area, rather than a military target.

More than 150 people were killed and the toll was likely to rise, according to Yohana Akol Ngor, the current minister of information in Abyei.

“What stood out was that bodies had been charred and reduced to ashes,” he said in an interview, adding that he had visited the market on Tuesday. “The victims were buried in two cemeteries.”

The medical charity Doctors Without Borders said that it was providing care to more than 20 people who had been wounded in the drone strikes, including several critical cases.

Local officials in Abyei blamed the Sudanese military for the attack, which South Sudan’s government condemned, summoning Sudan’s ambassador to the capital, Juba. A spokesman for the Sudanese military did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

Speaking in Qatar, President Emmanuel Macron railed against foreign leaders who he said had made false claims about unrest in France for their own political ends.

Listen

· 5:54 min

Video

Macron Says Foreign Leaders Shared Misinformation on France Protests

President Emmanuel Macron of France said President Trump and other foreign leaders made false claims about the protests in France.Credit Credit...Pool photo by Benoit Tessier

Oct. 21, 2026 Updated 3:16 p.m. ET

President Emmanuel Macron of France said on Wednesday that President Trump does not like France and that he was among the leaders who had made false claims about unrest there to advance their own political interests at France’s expense.

When asked whether Mr. Trump does not like France, Mr. Macron, addressing a group of reporters, said: “Well, one has to admit it. All the people who are speaking ill of our country right now are people who don’t like our country.”

Political leaders on both sides of the Atlantic “who echo what certain circles obviously want people to believe about what happened in France, they’re campaigning at our expense,” he said.

The worst rioting in years [shook France](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/world/europe/france-protests-riots.html) over the weekend, spinning off from demonstrations about [public education](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/world/europe/france-school-protest-paul-eluard.html) and [the rising cost of living](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/business/france-protests-bond-markets.html). Several government buildings were attacked and some were set on fire, nearly 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured, and more than 3,000 shops were looted or damaged, leading to the arrest of more than 2,500 people across France, officials said.

At a campaign rally in Kansas on Monday, two weeks before midterm U.S. elections, Mr. Trump said, “If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France, a once great nation that is being conquered, looted and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity.”

France’s government has accused “ultraleft militants” and opportunistic looters of causing the violence. The far-right, anti-immigration party, the National Rally, has [also accused the far left](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/france-far-right-protests-riots.html), which it said formed an alliance with “predators from the suburbs.” In France, “the suburbs” usually refers to working-class areas with large numbers of immigrants, primarily from Africa, and their descendants.

## In France, Raging Against the Luxury Machine

The looting of stores belonging to brands like Dior, Celine and Hermès has exposed a crack in the glossy facade.

Listen

· 6:09 min

![Image 1](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/21/multimedia/21ST-LUXURY-LOOTING-PARIS-1-pkgf/21ST-LUXURY-LOOTING-PARIS-1-pkgf-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

A vandalized Hermès storefront in Marseille, France, on Saturday.Credit...Thibaud Moritz/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Oct. 21, 2026 Updated 4:03 p.m. ET

Amid all of the images and videos that emerged of [the riots that took place in France](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/world/europe/france-protests-shock-arson.html) over the weekend, the most shocking are those of the clock tower collapsing in [Limoges](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/world/france-limoges-fire-arson-protests.html) after its 19th-century town hall was set alight.

Close behind, however, are the shots of looters storming the gates of luxury brands like [Celine](https://www.instagram.com/reels/DeoUAT_AWLv/), [Hermès](https://www.townandcountrymag.com/style/a74192069/luxury-goods-stolen-hermes-louis-vuitton-french-riots-2026/), [Louis Vuitton](https://x.com/staygroundeadtv/status/2111563981559390440) and [Saint Laurent](https://x.com/kumarsubodh_/status/2112033623792840845), breaking through the plate-glass windows that act as a scrim between the outside world and the hushed interiors that cater to the ultrarich, smashing their sparkling vitrines and looting their goods.

Of the estimated [more than 3,000 shops](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/world/europe/france-curfews-riots-protests-extended.html) that have been affected by the spiraling protests, including grocery stores, pharmacies and family-run operations, it is the luxury destruction that has caught much of the attention, and the imagination, of the watching world.

Whenever demonstrations are coupled with looting, they set off a conversation about wider, often inchoate, expressions of anger over inequality, not just in France but across the world. And though it would be easy to see this as yet another blip in a long history of using luxury products as a stand-in for social and economic injustice (one that stretches back to the French Revolution), it is also a response to a peculiarly contemporary reality the luxury industry itself has created.

The current situation is, after all, the third instance of physical attacks against luxury brands in the last eight years in the city that has styled itself the capital of luxury. In [2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pnetgThv5v0), during the movement against government pension reform, protesters stormed the doors of the LVMH headquarters on Avenue Montaigne in Paris, waving sparklers and ultimately burning an effigy of Bernard Arnault, the billionaire owner of the group (and that year briefly [the richest man in the world](https://www.forbes.com/sites/chasewithorn/2023/04/04/the-25-richest-people-in-the-world-2023/?sh=200f5b034969)).

Image

Cleaning up on Sunday outside a damaged Ralph Lauren store in Paris.Credit...Stephanie Lecocq/Reuters

## How We Draw Lines in a World Awash in A.I. Images

A Times reporter and editors discuss the challenges of sifting through what’s real and what’s not in pursuit of the news.

Listen

· 11:35 min

![Image 1](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/09/09/us/21insider-ai-images3/21insider-ai-images3-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

An A.I.-generated image posted to President Trump’s social media account recently.

Oct. 21, 2026, 9:21 a.m. ET

The internet is awash in A.I.-generated video and images — think President Trump appearing to tame a tiger or unbelievable fitness transformations.

But it’s rare for The New York Times to report on specific pieces of A.I. slop, even on days when a viral clip seems to be all anyone is talking about. Why is that? How do we decide to report on [certain](https://www.nytimes.com/video/technology/100000011001849/ai-influencers-health-supplements-fake-ads.html)[images](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/05/us/politics/trump-cinco-de-mayo-meme-jeffries-schumer.html)? And how do we know where to draw the line?

For answers, we turned to three colleagues who seek clarity in a bewildering media world: Stuart A. Thompson, who reports on online influence; Aisha Khan, the deputy Standards editor; and Mark Scheffler, who leads the Visual Investigations team.

These are edited excerpts from our conversation.

**How do we decide when A.I. images and memes are newsworthy?**

**STUART THOMPSON**: This is a tricky question! It’s one we’ve been debating since long before A.I. came along. Remember [QAnon](https://www.nytimes.com/article/what-is-qanon.html)? It was this massive online conspiracy theory, but there was a lot of debate about when, why and how mainstream media should weigh in.

My golden rule is that readers need to benefit from learning about it in some way. We don’t usually just debunk. We try to explain — usually focused on the causes and consequences. Who made it, why and how do they benefit? Who is harmed? The article needs to reflect something deeper about society, technology or regulations, I think. But it’s rarely obvious when to dive in.

**AISHA KHAN**: As Stuart says, figuring out when to report on these can be tricky. Is it the president, or a major political candidate, sharing an A.I.-generated video or [image of himself](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/03/us/politics/trump-pope-photo.html) or a rival to [make a political point](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/10/21/business/media/trump-ai-truth-social-no-kings.html)? Are [film studios turning to A.I.](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/18/technology/dor-video-studio-ai.html), or are propaganda operations [churning out A.I. content](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/technology/russian-propaganda-ai-war-songs.html)? What about those [strange videos on YouTube Kids](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/26/us/ai-videos-children-youtube.html)? Those are things we’d want to and have covered. But we also want to help our audience understand how the technology is evolving, and how to spot when someone is using A.I. to try to influence them or to sell them something.

**MARK SCHEFFLER**: We typically jump in when the imagery is purporting to show an incident or event with high stakes. A bombing of a building, someone appearing to perpetrate violence, attempts to deceive as part of a scam of some kind, whether it’s hawking a dubious product or trying to influence minors or other vulnerable populations. If there’s an accountability dimension, that’s when, from our perspective, it’s important for our team to cover it.

**We’ve reported on how A.I. imagery is changing elections like the****[Los Angeles mayoral race](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/21/us/spencer-pratt-ai-videos.html)****and global affairs like the****[Iran war](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/04/25/business/iran-trump-israel-war-memes.html)****. Where’s the line between showing our audience what we’re talking about and amplifying misinformation or disinformation?**

**AISHA**: This is a really difficult question, and one we wrestle with nearly every day. So much misinformation and disinformation is visual, now that it is easy to pump out A.I.-generated content. We don’t want to contribute to the circulation of dubious content created to mislead and sow confusion. So we take steps to choose clips and images with great care and restraint, limit what we show, and also label and mark content that is false. We also put a lot of effort into explaining and contextualizing anything we do show. And in some cases, we may decide it is better to explain the content rather than show it, for example if it is [very offensive](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/06/us/politics/trump-obamas-video-apes-truth-social.html).

**STUART**: I prefer showing readers the content as much as possible, except for content that is vulgar or deeply offensive. The imagery and videos I see on social media are sometimes shocking, and we risk sanitizing the reality of what people are doing with A.I. tools if we write about it only obliquely. Once you see it, you understand how far things have gone. But that leads to some tough conversations inside the newsroom, since we’re also wary of amplifying something false or doing a liar’s work for them by spreading the message further.

A politician publishing an A.I. fake would have been unthinkable a few years ago. Now there are hundreds of ads floating around the midterms that are A.I.-made. We probably need to find some broader significance to an A.I. fake to consider reporting on it. There was an A.I.-generated photo of President Trump seemingly embracing an aide on a golf course. It was nothing spectacular as far as A.I. fakes go, but people started to share it as though it was real. It fed into larger speculation among critics about the aide’s relationship to Mr. Trump. It was also apparently manipulated to remove the invisible watermarks that companies insert to identify A.I. imagery. So those methods, and the power of that particular image to fit within existing narratives, were all [worthy of an article](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/22/business/trump-natalie-harp-photo-ai.html).

**MARK:** The world is becoming awash in this material, and it’s getting more and more sophisticated. We are in a situation where objective reality is constantly being put into question and in some cases, wholly undermined. It’s important that we stay vigilant for synthetic content in our own reporting, but also continue to help people understand what it looks like and how it’s getting better and better at mimicking real-world scenes, locations, actions and people. [Stuart’s work](https://www.nytimes.com/by/stuart-a-thompson) in this space is invaluable.

**How do our considerations change when a world leader like President Trump posts an A.I. video?**

**AISHA**: The president posts a lot of videos, and not all are newsworthy. But he is the head of government, and some of his posts are definitely important to cover: when they are part of a campaign or promoting a policy platform, or might be misleading on an important issue. Our readers rely on us to report on these in a straightforward and responsible way, and to make it clear why they are newsworthy and to include any information they need to understand them.

**MARK**: To Aisha’s point, some of these posts have more serious consequences than others, but Mr. Trump has put A.I. slop into the public discourse at the highest levels now, and we should be persistent in calling out what it is, what it might reveal and what the downstream ramifications could be.

**STUART**: He’s the leader of the free world. What he is doing matters. We also risk becoming desensitized to his behavior. In some ways we already are. The first A.I.-generated video he posted was national news. Now people barely blink.

**A.I. videos generated for propaganda purposes may be outrageous, but many are clearly fake to a reasonable viewer — think Trump bombing protesters with excrement. How do our decisions about covering that type of video differ from reporting on deepfakes?**

**STUART**: At the beginning of this new A.I. age, watchdogs worried that A.I. deepfakes would flood the internet. What we got instead were a lot of memes, and relatively fewer deceptive deepfakes. But memes still have a lot of power. It’s less about debunking them than understanding what they’re being used for, and why.

**MARK**: I agree with Stuart that things that are more reflections of what people want to believe — whether they’re ludicrously presented or obviously fake — can still get a lot of traction. That’s harder to determine and report out, but it’s key.

**Are there best practices for displaying manipulated images that make news?**
